lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.title: Guided practice B: common probabilistic reasoning errors

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Read once, then cover the example and try the guided set from memory.

items.prompt: P(delay | rain) = P(delay). What does that mean?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A box holds 7 items, of which 3 are defective. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are defective, in lowest terms.
Given P(A and B) = 11/20 and P(B) = 13/20, find P(A | B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
Given P(A) = 32/100, P(B) = 29/100, and P(A and B) = 11/100, find P(A or B) in lowest terms.
In a study, P(has the condition | tested positive) is much smaller than P(tested positive | has the condition). What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The two conditional probabilities condition on different events, so they need not be close; a rare condition makes the first much smaller.
The relationship proves that one event causes the other.
The two conditional probabilities are equal, so the order of conditioning never matters.
The two events are mutually exclusive.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A box holds 11 items, of which 7 are defective. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are defective, in lowest terms.
Given P(A and B) = 10/100 and P(B) = 59/100, find P(A | B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
Given P(A) = 23/100, P(B) = 19/100, and P(A and B) = 9/100, find P(A or B) in lowest terms.
In a study, the probability of a delay is the same whether or not it is raining. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The two conditional probabilities are equal, so the order of conditioning never matters.
Delay and rain are independent, because conditioning on rain does not change the probability of a delay.
The relationship proves that one event causes the other.
The two events are mutually exclusive.
